title: How to Think About High-Level System Design

sections.heading: Everyday Analogy
sections.body: Think of an app like a city. High-Level Design (HLD) is the city map before building roads and buildings. It shows big pieces — where users enter, where data lives, how parts talk — without tiny code details. System Design interview questions ask you to draw this map.

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.body:
Why it exists: real apps serve millions. We group problems so you can reuse maps:
- Core Infrastructure: Rate Limiting (blocking too many requests) and Distributed Key-Value Store (many computers acting as one simple storage)
- Social Feeds + Messaging + Streaming: Social Graph, News Feed, Real-time Chat. Same map fits many apps.

sections.heading: What can go wrong
sections.body: What can go wrong: if traffic jumps 100x, bottlenecks appear. Rate Limiter fails and lets flood through, or blocks real users. Key-Value Store runs out of space or slows. News Feed becomes stale or late. Practice on a whiteboard, like Excalidraw, helps you spot these cracks before users do.

steps.narration: Users send many requests, like cars entering a city.
Rate Limiter gate decides if request can pass or must wait.
App service does the work using shared building blocks.
Distributed Key-Value Store keeps simple data across many machines.
Feed or chat system sends the right updates back to users.

quiz.q: What is High-Level Design (HLD) most like?
options: Drawing a city map of big parts before building
quiz.why: HLD is the big-picture map showing where users enter, where data lives, and how parts talk.

quiz.q: What fails first if usage grows 100x and you have no Rate Limiter?
options: Servers get flooded, slow down, and may crash
quiz.why: Without Rate Limiting, too many requests overwhelm services and storage — a classic bottleneck.

quiz.q: Why are HLD questions grouped into domains like Social Feeds and Messaging?
options: To reuse similar maps for similar problems
Because every app is totally unique
quiz.why: Grouping lets you reuse core patterns like feed, graph, and real-time delivery across many apps.
